Fakeboot

Someone cloned real shoe-repair shops to rip off their customers. This is what I found when I followed the money.

Investigated by Paul Romeo, an outside researcher · the real shops are victims, not suspects

See the network Meet the fake shops

Here's the scam in three sentences. Someone builds a convincing copy of a real local shoe-repair shop's website — same name, same street address. You find it through Google, it looks legit, you place an order. But when you hit the checkout button, your payment doesn't go to that shop at all: it goes to a completely different website run by whoever built the fakes.

I call those checkout sites cash registers — the place the money actually lands. Fourteen fake shops feed into eight of them, and the registers share fingerprints (same office address, same software) that point back to one operation. The real shops just keep getting angry phone calls about orders they never took.

Where your money actually goes

Google Maps

How the fakes find their victims

The nastiest part: on Google Maps, the real shops' own listings have been edited to point at the fake websites. You look up a cobbler you trust, Maps hands you the impostor. I've filed corrections for the confirmed ones; the rest are documented below as evidence.

Correction requests submitted for National Shoe Services, Chicago Cobblers Dynasty, Nu-Way Shoe Repair, and Verona Leather Shoe. The rest are parked until Google acts on the first batch — the fake links stay documented here either way, because a dead link on a real shop's listing still confuses customers.
